I've had anxiety problems for longer than I can remember, but two episodes come to mind, one recently occurring, and the other a year ago. The experience a year ago was probably my worst episode of anxiety. Up until that moment, I had never experienced it that bad, but when I did experience it, my mind was consumed by some approaching doom, and I could not calm myself down, and ended up just escaping to my place of comfort. I experienced a fear of such intensity, that I could not properly comprehend my situation. Currently, I am experiencing a more mild version of anxiety, but much more lasting. I have put such pressure on myself over my life that I am constantly anxious about failing, and letting my family down. Anxiety sucks, and I can't seem to stop it, so I guess it'll just be a part of me.

I assume you have seen a therapist. Can I ask if doing so has helped alleviate your anxiety? Or at least helped you identify the cause?

I saw a therapist when my anxiety was panic attacks maybe once a week. Since then I have discontinued. I've been thinking about going back. I say go to a therapist because they are educated and trained to help people with anxiety/ anxiety disorders. I've been trying to keep it under control by researching and trying different methods of living with anxiety but I would never devalue the opinion of a psychiatrist. It's worth it to try for a while and see if it helps at all. If I were to identify the cause of my anxiety it would be my OCD and upbringing. As of yet I haven't had these linked to anxiety but my psychiatrist confirmed that my upbringing has led to other complications in how I view myself and how I interact with others and the world.

Also struggled with anxiety my whole life. Escaping to your place of comfort is good and helps a ton- once you're there you can try and directly confront your anxiety. Try and separate yourself from your life for a moment, and take a third person omniscient perspective (you know everything about the situation and yourself, but aren't directly involved). From here try and identify what, if anything, is causing your anxiety. School, work, friends, loved ones?

If you can't think of any reason why you're anxious, then you need to convince yourself there's no reason to be anxious. At that point you're in control and can chill.

Say you've identified why you're anxious in the moment. What, relative to that reason, are you in control of? Hypothetically it's an upcoming party. You don't know who will be there, what you'll be doing, or how long it'll go. So those things are out of your control. Don't worry about them, convince yourself that there's nothing you can do to change them so there's no reason to waste time and energy worrying. What do you have control of? How you dress, react, participate, drink, dance, talk, and interact are good examples. These are all things you can affect, and should try to improve in the moment. Put some thought into dressing well, who you're comfortable with, what situations to try and avoid, and what you can do if you find yourself in one of those situations.

Once you've tried and improved everything you're in control of, you're as well prepared as you can be. Yes, something might go wrong, but at this point it won't be your fault; you've taken control of everything you can. Go and have fun.

Recognizing what I'm in control of and what is outside of my control has helped me immensely- it takes most of the guesswork out of things that make me anxious, and allows me to feel like I'm in charge of how something goes. That's my 2 cents, hope it helps.

Thank you for your suggestions! I can see the benefit of looking at my anxiety objectively, to distinguish the cause. The idea of control is also important, as you say. As far as my experience has shown me, my anxiety emerges from situations that I am not in control of. I understand that there is no reason to be anxious about things that are out of one's control, but the anxiety is there. I guess my problem is that I unfairly blame myself for things that are out of my control. The worst part of my anxiety is the catastrophising. When I am about to do something, or in the process of doing something, a thought will appear, suggesting what if something goes wrong. This thought will grow and grow, until I eventually avoid doing the 'thing' in fear of the something going wrong. Thanks for sparking this train of thought, as it has helped me think it through for once!

I completely relate to this. @mwg gave some excellent advice, and that's what worked for me in the past, but I became so focused on controlling everything I could that I ended up going to the "catastrophising." Always thinking about and being prepared for the worst possible scenario so I can try to control as much of it as possible.

I'm still working on that, but I've found something similar to what @mwg said usually works, or at least helps. You have to convince yourself that not everything will turn into a disaster. And even if it does, you'll be capable of dealing with it, will survive it and move on. You don't have a crystal ball, you have absolutely no idea what's gonna happen.

When it comes down to it, driving yourself crazy over it accomplishes absolutely nothing. You can't anticipate or control the external shit that happens, but you can control how much you allow it to affect you internally (in your head that is).

It's kinda corny but there's a pretty well known quote I repeat in my head a lot too. "Never take life seriously, nobody gets out alive anyway." I use it to remind myself that the vast majority of shit I drive myself crazy over, really doesn't matter as much as I think it does and not to spend my time driving myself crazy over nonsense.
